name: Victor Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the late team handling cancelled utility accounts. When a customer has called four times about the same closing bill, I find the entry that made the account stick and explain it to the newer agent. My two-year college diploma taught me the books, but years on this queue made me one of the best at untangling them. I earn the usual rate for a lead, not a bonus for every mistake I catch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who depends on that wage at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Eleni works in a grocery warehouse, and we have two children, ten and fifteen, plus a mortgage. We have about four months of expenses saved, though a boiler repair could take a chunk of it. Some other contact centres are within reach. I use the approved AI search occasionally after colleagues show that a case type is reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the late team that a quicker summary is welcome, provided the person signing the final bill reads it. Customers deserve a name on a correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work and pay would hold. Four months saved lets us breathe, although the mortgage and that old boiler mean we cannot treat the reserve as spare cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep reviewing closing bills and make a note when the search tool misses a final payment. In the first year I will keep adding a little from each wage to the boiler reserve before we book another weekend away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work, mildly watchful about the house. A boiler does not care whether AI had a good year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the summary is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I send it back to the agent with the account date marked, then sign the correction after they fix it. The person whose bill was wrong gets a call, not just another automated message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask others to record errors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the same mistake keeps recurring. A lone odd bill is my job to fix; repeated errors would need a shared record for management.

say: I would welcome **faster summaries** if a person checks the final bill.
I would insist customers get a **named correction**.
think: I expect my **lead role** and typical pay to hold.
I treat **four months saved** as mortgage and boiler protection.
do: Keep reviewing **closing bills** and flag final-payment errors.
Add wages to the **boiler reserve** before another weekend trip.
feel: **Calm** about work, watchful about house costs.
S0.quote: A boiler does not care whether AI had a good year.
fieldNote: He is a **skilled lead** on typical pay.

He uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues prove a case type.

steps.text: Keep reviewing closing bills and marking search-tool payment errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that closing a chat is not the same as settling a disputed bill. We should ask for a measure that includes corrections and a fair rota for the people left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the routine cancellations to move to software and some paid shifts to go. I may keep the complicated accounts, but fewer lead hours would still change our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will compare the approved assistant with twenty closed account cases and record its wrong dates. I will bring the results to our union branch with two late-shift colleagues; together we will ask management for written staffing plans and paid time for corrections. If my hours fall in the first year, I will apply for posted paid dispute roles at other centres only if written wages and hours cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the rota, though four months saved gives us time to check an offer. I would rather count errors with colleagues than guess at management plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it becomes required, I will learn its review view from a trained agent during paid shifts and practise on closed accounts. I will not sign a live correction on my first try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a higher title persuade you to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without the full weekly rate in writing. Eleni and I also have to see whether the new late shifts fit school pickup and her warehouse rota.

I would bring **wrong-date counts** to our union branch.
think: I expect **routine chats** and paid shifts to shrink.
I know fewer **lead hours** would press our mortgage budget.
do: Test **twenty closed accounts** and learn required review controls on paid shifts.
Join **late-shift colleagues** through the union to request staffing and correction time.
Apply after cuts for **posted paid disputes** with written mortgage-covering wages, hours and school pickup.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, with some search time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our branch that full thinking AI by 2028 could clear most utility calls. Robots around 2031 are a separate date, not extra time for the headset jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the late team could be closed and my lead wage with it. Four months saved buys a search, but Eleni’s warehouse pay cannot carry the mortgage and children alone for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will ask for written notice dates and put the planned bathroom work on hold while the plumbing is safe. My colleagues and I will ask the union to seek paid redeployment terms. If my role ends in the first year after 2028, I will apply for posted paid account-audit work only where written wages and hours cover our mortgage and fit the children’s school routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed by the speed. Four months can disappear while people argue over which department owns a case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is account audit safe under general AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It is another screen job and could be a short bridge, but I know the records and might earn a wage while we search further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a qualification now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete a required audit course only for a real posted paid vacancy that funds the fees and pays the study time. The bathroom money cannot be a tuition fund.

say: I would warn **2028 AGI** threatens utility calls.
I would tell our **union branch** that robots arrive later.
think: I expect our **late team** and my wage could disappear.
I know four months saved cannot replace my **lead wage** while Eleni pays the mortgage.
do: Request **written notice** and delay bathroom work only while plumbing remains safe.
Seek **union redeployment terms**; complete funded required audit training on paid time only for a posted paid vacancy.
Apply after job loss for **posted paid audit work** only with written mortgage-covering wages and hours fitting school routine.
S2.quote: The bathroom money cannot be a tuition fund.
fieldNote: He treats **audit work** as a paid bridge, not a permanent refuge.
His **course condition** includes a posted vacancy, funded fees and paid time.
He delays bathroom work only while **plumbing remains safe**.

steps.text: Delay bathroom work only while the plumbing stays safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us bargain for a route before the calls disappear. General AI reaches the screen in 2031, and hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep the difficult bills until 2031, but I want a second skill while the current wage comes in. The reserve gives me a little time; it cannot pay for a bad move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will ask the employer for a paid shadow day in account audit if it posts a place. If a posted paid audit role covers our mortgage and school hours and funds its required course on paid time, I will complete it. In the first year after 2031 I will move only on a written offer meeting those wages and hours, after Eleni and I compare both rotas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the extra years let me see a real job before signing up. A course name is not a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would join other leads in asking for written access rules to the paid shadow days, so managers cannot hand them only to their favourites. We would ask for hours to be protected while we train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no audit opening appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep my present lead hours while they exist and check other centres. I will not spend four months of savings pretending an unposted role exists.

I would distinguish **2031 screens** from later robots.

feel: **Anxious**, with time to verify a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team ten years is enough to build options, if paid shifts stay long enough to fund them. General AI reaches calls in 2036, with hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still owe the mortgage, though the children could need less ferrying. I want six months of expenses saved before a risky change, rather than a certificate bought with debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will keep the lead shift and put part of each pay toward six months saved. Once a year I will compare posted audit and centre roles with their full weekly rates. If my call hours fall in the first year after 2036, I will move only for a written paid offer with wages and hours covering the mortgage, after Eleni and I check our household rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about where calls end up, but steadier about having time. We could save from real wages instead of betting the house on a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the savings target slips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Eleni’s hours or mine fall, the six-month target moves back. I will not call borrowed money a reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in a union as your job changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would keep my membership while I work, because pay and training rules still need collective scrutiny. That does not mean I think any one course will save us.

I would separate **2036 call risk** from later robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The late team could vanish before any paid audit places exist. Written notice, paid redeployment and a real posted job with mortgage-covering hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a correction still has a person’s name on it after the software closes a bill. The customer cannot take a chatbot’s signature to a payment desk.

headlineQuote: The customer cannot take a chatbot’s signature to a payment desk.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old skilled lead** with a two-year college diploma and typical pay.
He has a **mortgage and two children**, about four months saved and some nearby contact centres.
He uses **AI occasionally** after coworkers test it and favours union bargaining over private guesses.
He seeks **posted paid audit work** only with funded training and written household-covering terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his late-team wage before paid audit jobs appear.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid redeployment and a posted mortgage-covering job would help.
